title: A Radiators for the Aftermath
premise: Wren Kavanagh, a bridge inspector who measures everything and feels nothing measurable, hears an unrecorded song on the radio — one written years ago by their estranged brother, who died before it could exist. The broadcast is impossible, and tracing it pulls Wren into the orbit of the small pirate station that aired it and the people who loved the brother Wren abandoned. As Wren investigates whether the song was stolen, leaked, or haunted, they must decide between protecting the station's fragile community of loyalists and exposing the truth about how the recording survived. In the end, Wren translates the sentence their brother left unfinished — 'you were always the bridge' — chooses truth over loyalty by testifying to what really happened, and catches the last bus back to a neighborhood that no longer needs them but finally sees them.
about_author: E. M. Ravensworth is the pen name of a former municipal engineer who spent eleven years inspecting steel truss bridges across the industrial Midwest before turning to fiction. Their work examines the quiet mathematics of grief, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Third-person limited from Wren's POV. Wren inspects the Halvorsen Bridge, measuring millimeters of drift in its joints while deflecting a coworker's friendly questions with practiced smiles. At home, a late-night radio program plays a song Wren has never heard but instantly recognizes as their dead brother Teo's handwriting in melody. Emotional beat: the crack in a sealed life.

chapters.title: The Frequency That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Obsessively re-tuning, Wren confirms the song is real, recorded, and aired on a low-power pirate station called Lighthouse 104. They drive to the old neighborhood for the first time in nine years and find the station broadcasting from a decommissioned water tower. Emotional beat: dread braided with longing; the past has a signal strength.

chapters.title: People Who Keep Lights On
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Marisol Vega, the station's founder. She introduces the volunteer crew who run Lighthouse 104 — archivists of music never meant to be heard. She recognizes Wren's surname immediately but says nothing. Emotional beat: warmth offered to someone who came to take something.

chapters.title: What Teo Left in the Walls
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Searching Teo's old rehearsal space above a laundromat, Wren finds reel-to-reel tapes hidden in insulation and a notebook containing a single untranslated sentence in a private language the siblings invented as children. Emotional beat: guilt made physical; every object accuses gently.

chapters.title: The Man Who Claims the Song
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A record producer named Dale Pruitt arrives claiming he legally acquired Teo's catalog after his death and threatens the station with FCC complaints and lawsuits. Marisol suspects he obtained the tapes through means no court would bless. Emotional beat: the law arrives wearing a smile like Wren's own.

chapters.title: Loyalty Is a Load-Bearing Wall
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The crew asks Wren to help hide the master tapes rather than let Pruitt seize them. Wren agrees, lying to Marisol about what they know: that Teo mailed the recordings to Pruitt deliberately, hoping to be discovered posthumously. Emotional beat: complicity; Wren becomes the thing they inspect for cracks.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol discovers Wren's deception and confronts them at the water tower during a storm. Wren finally decodes the sibling-language sentence aloud: 'You were always the bridge' — Teo's forgiveness and accusation at once. Emotional beat: climax of identity; Wren admits they reported Teo's unpaid debts years ago, the wound that broke them apart.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Choosing truth over the crew's loyalty, Wren gives a sworn statement revealing how Pruitt actually obtained the tapes — through a predatory debt collector, not Teo — invalidating his claim. The crew feels betrayed by the process even as it saves them. Emotional beat: justice outside the law costs the justice inside friendship.

chapters.title: Signal Fade
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The station loses its tower lease anyway; the last broadcast approaches. Pruitt, exposed, quietly withdraws. Marisol offers Wren the master tapes and something harder: an honest accounting of who Teo was beyond Wren's guilt. Emotional beat: grief allowed to be ordinary instead of monumental.

chapters.title: The Last Bus to the Old Neighborhood
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The route is permanently rerouted; Wren rides its final run end to end, holding the tapes, listening to the whole song at last. At the terminus, Marisol waits with coffee. Wren doesn't smile to end the conversation — they begin one. Emotional beat: resolution; the bridge holds because it moves.
